name: Sustaining Change Over Years
title: Sustaining Change Over Years
answer: Sustaining change over years means building durable habits of governance, measurement and honest reporting rather than chasing each new AI tool, because the tools will keep changing and the rules and practices will need updating. The habits matter more than any particular product, and they are what make adoption last. Districts that hold these habits adapt more easily than those that react to every new tool.

sections.body: This idea is about how a school system keeps its AI practices alive across time rather than treating adoption as a one-off project. AI tools will keep changing, so the rules and practices set out in this Volume will need updating, which means a district needs a way of revising its work rather than a fixed answer. The problem it solves is that adoption fades when it depends on a single product or a single enthusiastic leader. A district with strong habits of governance, measurement and honest reporting can absorb change more easily than one that chases each new tool. The habits, not the product, are what make adoption last.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the work is to keep the habits running rather than to keep buying. Districts should revisit their AI strategy at least once a year, and the annual report is a natural moment for that review. Leaders can ask what worked, what did not, what has changed in the tools and the law, and what to do next. Written rules, published results and a committee with broad membership help practices survive changes in leadership, and so does a staff that understands why the practices matter. The text does not set out separate versions of this work by grade band, so the same cycle of annual review and honest reporting applies across a district rather than differing by year group.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it presents instead is a claim about durability: that a district building strong habits of governance, measurement and honest reporting will adapt more easily than one that chases each new tool, and that the habits matter more than any particular product. It also names leadership turnover as a threat to lasting change, noting that a new superintendent or principal may abandon what came before. The suggested countermeasures are written rules, published results, a committee with broad membership and a staff that understands why the practices matter. The recommendation to revisit strategy at least once a year, using the annual report as the moment, is likewise presented as practice rather than as a tested finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about continuity and honesty rather than about any tool. Leadership turnover is the named risk, because a new superintendent or principal may abandon what came before, which is why written rules, published results and a broadly composed committee matter. The text also assumes that staff understand why the practices matter, since that understanding is part of what helps practices survive. The decisions stay with people: leaders are the ones who ask what worked, what did not, what has changed in the tools and the law, and what to do next. Nothing in the text hands those judgements to a product, and the annual review is described as steady and honest rather than automatic.
